For fifty years the cricket pavilion at Askerby sat at the bottom of the village field, a few yards from the river Lume: a plain timber building of 1911, with a veranda, two changing rooms and a tea room. In March 1962 a gale tore away half its roof. The committee met in April, and the secretary, Moira Callan, wrote down nearly every word.

The first thing discussed was the river. In 1947 the Lume had lain a foot deep in the changing rooms for three days, and Tobias Fenn, the groundsman, had spent the following week shovelling silt out of them with two younger members. He had distrusted the site ever since. Money was a separate worry. The club had been in debt since 1958, when a new scoreboard cost twice what Harlan Dace, the builder, had quoted, and rot was already in its posts.

Dace came with an offer. He worked mostly in brick, he said, but the timber was worth forty pounds to him if the club would sell. Then Fenn rose with a plan of his own. At the north end of the field, where the ground climbed toward a stand of beeches, the pavilion could be jacked up, set on rollers and hauled to higher ground.

The captain, Neil Pryor, argued that the gale's damage was only to the sheeting and could be repaired where it stood, but the vote went nine to four for Fenn's plan, and both of his shovelling partners were among the nine. Dace was paid to do the hauling, which took six weeks instead of two and cracked the floor in two places. Agnes Rowe, the headmistress, let the club use the village school hall for the rest of the season.

The Lume has kept to its banks every year since. The pavilion sits up among the beeches, on a floor that still tilts. Reading the minutes, it is hard to escape the sense that the committee spent its savings fleeing a river that had visited once in thirty-five years, and that the club went on paying for one frightened week long after the water had gone.

Last October the Brannock Reservoir dropped two meters over a month, though Hester Vane, the engineer in charge of the dam, had first set a schedule of four days for repairing its gates. The drop would leave Hollin Cove, a shallow arm with a worn gravel bar across its mouth, nearly dry; only the old river channel would stay deep. On the cove's floor lived some four thousand mussels, counted that summer by the biologist Ilse Marrow and her student Teo Arlan. A mussel can follow a falling waterline on its single foot, but slowly, about a meter a day.

The reservoir had been lowered once before, twenty years earlier, and Bram Kettle, a fisherman from Wendle, recorded it in the logbook he has kept for thirty years. That time a jammed gate let the water out slowly, over five weeks. His log describes long furrows across the mud, each ending in a live mussel at the water's edge, and he counted barely a dozen dead.

It was Vane who proposed the plan the team followed. Instead of opening the gates wide, she raised the drop's length from four days to thirty, so the water would fall about as fast as a mussel crawls. Kettle had offered to round up volunteers to carry mussels out in buckets, and Teo had sketched a wall of sandbags across the cove's mouth, but Vane's plan needed neither. Odile Prask, who runs the breeding hatchery at Sallow Ford, took two hundred mussels into her tanks as a reserve.

For a month the mussels crept after the water. Marrow tagged a hundred and found ninety of them alive at the new waterline when the drop ended, and Teo, walking the cove's floor, counted fewer than three hundred stranded behind. The repair crew was paid to wait, and finished the gates in the November storms, three weeks late and over budget.

A month of a hired crew's wages and a repair rushed through November gales is a steep price for a rescue built on one fisherman's note about one jammed gate, when forty people with buckets could have cleared the cove in four days.
